name: Financial District
short_description: Manhattan neighborhood, south of Chambers St. Not in existing POI list (which holds specific landmarks). Flagged new_poi for user triage.
_poi_role_reasoning: A neighborhood (radius 400) of canyons and streets you move through, a contextual diffuse area.
_poi_role_source: Suited traders pouring onto the streets at 5pm in the financial canyons

beats.script_body: Up until the 19th century, life in New York City was primarily concentrated in what is now Lower Manhattan. Around 1700, the city barely extended beyond Fulton Street, and a hundred years later only a handful of additional apartment blocks had been built. When City Hall opened in 1812 it seemed unimaginable that the city might continue growing to the north.

name: Chinatown
_poi_role_reasoning: A large neighborhood (radius 350) experienced as you move through its sensory streets, a contextual area.
_poi_role_source: the dense crowds on the streets, the awnings with Chinese characters

beats.script_body: At the end of the 19th century, Chinatown was often the scene for fighting street gangs, such as the Dead Rabbits and the Bowery Boys. Apartments in what is today Columbus Park garnered notorious nicknames such as Bone Alley, Kerosene Row, and Bandits' Roost. Chinatown has long since shaken off this reputation; today the dynamic neighborhood is a popular destination thanks to its plethora of stores and restaurants.

name: Lower East Side
_poi_role_reasoning: A large neighborhood (radius 400) walked along its immigrant-era streets, a contextual area.
_poi_role_source: Old-world fabric and luggage stores along Orchard Street

beats.script_body: Some 200 years ago the Lower East Side was flooded with immigrants, and the Lower East Side Tenement Museum on Orchard Street is an excellent place to gain insight into the history of the neighborhood. When walking around, don't forget to look up from time to time to see the beautiful brick buildings with those great fire escapes that are so characteristic of New York City.

physical_cues.cue: Brick buildings with the iron fire escapes characteristic of New York; look up

beats.source_passage: Some 200 years ago the Lower East Side was flooded with immigrants, and the Lower East Side Tenement Museum on Orchard Street is an excellent place to gain insight into the history of the neighborhood. Today many young people are attracted to the happening (night) scene and trendy bars, cafés, and boutiques. With its numerous galleries, the neighborhood also appeals to art aficionados. When walking around, don't forget to look up from time to time to see the beautiful brick buildings with those great fire escapes that are so characteristic of New York City.

name: Jane's Carousel
short_description: A lovingly restored 1922 carousel by the Philadelphia Toboggan Company, housed in a Jean Nouvel acrylic pavilion at the north end of Brooklyn Bridge Park in Dumbo.
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete carousel in a pavilion, explicitly a named sub-feature at the north end of Brooklyn Bridge Park.
_poi_role_source: The star attraction of the north end of Brooklyn Bridge Park is a vintage carousel

beats.script_body: Jane's Carousel dates back to 1922. For years it operated in Youngstown, Ohio. The developer of the park where it currently stands bought it in 1983, together with his wife, Jane. After years of renovation it was restored to its original glory, and Jane's Carousel reopened in 2011. Now young and old can enjoy a ride for a fair price.

physical_cues.cue: The restored 1922 carousel in its glass pavilion at Old Dock Street

name: Staten Island Ferry
short_description: Iconic free ferry, Wikipedia article, millions of riders, famous free Statue of Liberty views. High gravity. Geocoded to Manhattan (Whitehall) terminal.
_poi_role_reasoning: Geocoded to the Whitehall terminal you board at; a discrete embarkation point rather than an area you walk through.
_poi_role_source: The right side at the back of the ferry for the Manhattan skyline view

beats.script_body: A ride on the Staten Island Ferry is a fun and free way to see the Statue of Liberty and the New York City skyline. Aside from the occasional savvy tourist, the ferry is primarily used by commuters from Staten Island. All told, a trip to Staten Island and back takes about an hour, and you never have to wait too long for the next boat.

name: Castle Clinton
short_description: Tier-4/5 candidate: National Monument, former fort/Castle Garden/aquarium/immigration depot. Major historic landmark inside Battery Park.
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete circular fort building inside Battery Park; small radius and 'go inside' building cue make it a sub-feature stop.
_poi_role_source: The circular stone building you can go inside if it is open

beats.script_body: Castle Clinton was built on a man-made island and completed in 1811. Its initial purpose was to protect the harbor from the British. Later it functioned as a theater and then as a landing depot for immigrants — between 1855 and 1890, some 8 million immigrants passed through here. For a time after that, the castle was even home to the New York Aquarium. Today you can purchase tickets here for the ferry over to the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island.

physical_cues.cue: The circular fort of Castle Clinton on its former man-made island at the edge of Battery Park

beats.poi_name: National Museum of the American Indian
beats.script_body: On the site where Fort Amsterdam stood during the 17th century now stands the US Custom House, whose first three stories house the National Museum of the American Indian. The custom house was completed in 1907, at a time when the Port of New York was the most important port in the United States — sixty percent of all customs duties in the country were collected here.

physical_cues.cue: The grand US Custom House facade on Bowling Green, housing the museum in its lower stories

name: Federal Hall
short_description: Tier-5 candidate: Washington's first inauguration site, Zenger trial, Stamp Act Congress, first US Congress / Bill of Rights. Greek Revival landmark, George Washington statue.
_poi_role_reasoning: Discrete Greek Revival landmark building you stand before.
_poi_role_source: Note the statue of George Washington: it was here... Greek Revival edifice

beats.script_body: Federal Hall National Memorial stands on the site where George Washington took the oath of office as the first U.S. president and where the first Congress convened. The current building was previously a U.S. customs house and once contained more than three hundred million dollars in silver and gold. Today it is a museum about Washington's inauguration, freedom of the press, and Federal Hall — the first capitol, which stood on this spot.

physical_cues.cue: The Greek-temple facade and steps of Federal Hall at 26 Wall Street, where Washington was inaugurated

name: Trinity Church
short_description: Tier-5 candidate: Gothic Revival church and graveyard, Alexander Hamilton's grave. Very high gravity. NOTE: chunk cross-references full description to p.183 (another chunk) — minimal content here.
_poi_role_reasoning: A single church and its adjacent graveyard you stand at; small radius, object-focused cues.

beats.script_body: Trinity Church is a charming, beautiful, old example of Neo-Gothic architecture, which miraculously was unscathed after 9/11. Alexander Hamilton is buried in the cemetery, as well as a few of the earliest Dutch colonists.

physical_cues.cue: Trinity Church's Neo-Gothic spire and the churchyard graves at the head of Wall Street

name: St. Paul's Chapel
short_description: Oldest church building in Manhattan (1766), Wikipedia article, George Washington connection, 9/11 relief site. Moderate-high gravity.
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete church building you stand before and enter; small radius.
_poi_role_source: The Ionic columns and huge pediment of the facade

beats.script_body: St. Paul's Chapel has miraculously survived the Revolutionary War and two terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center relatively unaltered. In the hours, weeks, and months that followed 9/11, the chapel became a place where rescue and recovery workers from Ground Zero received care and support. Visitors can see photos and read stories from this time inside the chapel.

physical_cues.cue: Photos and stories from the 9/11 recovery effort displayed inside the chapel

name: 9/11 Memorial and Museum
short_description: Top-tier global landmark. Full Wikipedia article, primary Frommer's headline sight, ~3M+ annual visitors. Among NYC's most-visited attractions.
_poi_role_reasoning: A discrete museum and memorial you enter and stand within, with interior exhibit cues.
_poi_role_source: visitors descend down, down, down into this underground museum

beats.script_body: At the 9/11 Memorial Museum you can see an exhibition that presents the attack on the World Trade Center in three parts: the events of the day itself, the background leading up to that day, and the impact in the period that followed. The museum also regularly organizes films and lectures.

physical_cues.cue: The museum's exhibition halls below the memorial plaza

The museum also regularly organizes films and lectures.

name: City Hall
short_description: Federal-style seat of NYC government since 1812, with a coffered rotunda, the Governor's Room, and Washington's writing table on view via twice-weekly tours.
_poi_role_reasoning: A single government building with interior cues and tiny radius (10), a discrete destination.
_poi_role_source: the building's elegant coffered rotunda, the City Council chamber, and the Governor's Room

beats.script_body: City Hall houses the office of the mayor, the city council, and various other offices. There is a small collection of memorabilia on display in the building, and free tours are given during the week — though you must make a reservation for tours online.

physical_cues.cue: City Hall's facade across City Hall Park, off Broadway

name: Municipal Building
short_description: The monumental 1909 Manhattan Municipal Building at 1 Centre Street, built to add office space for city agencies and crowned by Adolph Weinman's gilded-copper statue 'Civic Fame,' whose five-pointed crown symbolizes the city's five boroughs.

beats.script_body: The awe-inspiring Municipal Building was built starting in 1909 to create additional office space for municipal agencies. The building is surmounted by the copper statue 'Civic Fame,' a female figure holding a five-pointed crown that symbolizes the five boroughs of the city.

name: Brooklyn Bridge
short_description: Iconic global landmark, extensive Wikipedia coverage, National Historic Landmark, millions of annual pedestrians. Top-tier gravity. Note: coordinate is mid-span; Manhattan-tower-specific trigger may warrant a sub-POI later.
_poi_role_reasoning: Large 120m radius and cues describe walking across/along the span rather than standing at one point.
_poi_role_source: Walking the span of the Brooklyn Bridge lets you see this marvel up close

beats.script_body: Construction of the 5,989-foot-long Brooklyn Bridge began in 1870 and was completed thirteen years later. The Gothic granite towers and steel cables are now an iconic New York City landmark. Walk out across the bridge for an amazing view of both Manhattan and Brooklyn, which is particularly beautiful at sunset.

physical_cues.cue: The Gothic granite towers and steel cables of the bridge; the walkway view of Manhattan and Brooklyn

name: Columbus Park
short_description: Leafy park at Mulberry and Bayard Sts in Chinatown where mah-jongg players, tai-chi practitioners, and locals gather; formerly the site of Five Points, NYC's first tenement slums.
_poi_role_reasoning: A park where people gather across the space (mah-jongg, tai-chi), narrated as an area; a named green space within Chinatown.
_poi_role_source: this leafy oasis is core to NYC history

beats.script_body: Columbus Park is located in what was once one of the worst neighborhoods in the city. Today, however, the park is the peaceful backdrop to scenes of women chatting over games of cards, men hunkering over Chinese checkerboards, and children playing. There is always lots of activity here.

physical_cues.cue: Card games, Chinese-checkerboard players, and children at play across Columbus Park

beats.script_body: Fraunces Tavern is more than just a bar and restaurant; it is also a museum where you can learn about the Revolutionary War. Founding Father George Washington and his officers celebrated their victory here with a festive dinner.

name: Stone Street
short_description: Tier-3/4 candidate: cobbled Greek Revival historic street, first paved street in New Amsterdam, 1835 fire rebuild. Distinctive streetscape.
_poi_role_reasoning: A historic cobbled streetscape experienced as you move along it rather than a single point.

beats.script_body: Stone Street gets its name from being the first paved road in the city. Today many restaurants fill its 19th-century buildings, and the street has become a popular spot among those who work on Wall Street. When the weather is nice, the restaurants set up wooden tables right in the middle of the street.

beats.script_body: At the Lower East Side Tenement Museum you can discover what life was like for millions of New York immigrants in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. To visit, you must sign up for a tour, and reservations beforehand are recommended.
